fixes.explanation: Servants do show up in this story, but his request isn't about running them. He asks, “Father, give me my share of the estate.” Later he plans to ask to be made like one of his father's hired servants (Luke 15:19). Running them isn't what he asks for.
Squandered is the word, friend. The younger son squandered his wealth in wild living. It means he spent what he had wastefully. It's the opposite of me guarding the last chocolate chip in the bowl.

Sharing would be a lovely thing to do with a fortune, but that's not the word the text uses. The text says he squandered his wealth in wild living. And when the hunger hit, no one would give him a thing (Luke 15:16).

Pigs. The man sends him into his fields to feed the pigs. A son who started with a share of the estate is now working for a citizen of that country. I think that's a long way down from where he started.
Grapes would be a different job, friend, but the text doesn't send him there. The citizen sends him into his fields to feed the pigs. No vineyard shows up in this story.
That's right. No one gives him food. The text says “…no one would give him a thing.” He's hungry enough to long for what the pigs are eating.
Doubt isn't what the text says, friend. It says the father “…was filled with compassion.” And then he runs to his son.
Pleads is the word. The father came out and pleaded with him. The older son refused to go in, so the father comes out to him.
That's what the father says. “Son, you are always with me… and all that is mine is yours.” Look at how he starts, with the word son. All that is the father's, he says, is the older son's.

Servants are in this story, but they're not who the father means. He says, “…this brother of yours was dead and is alive again…” One servant is the one who answers when the older son asks what's going on.
